Hello and welcome to the synopsis, a Speedwell research podcast. My name is Drew Cohen, and this week on the synopsis, we are going to be reading one of our Speedwell memos. This one is an excerpt from our coupon research report, which if you want the full report, you can find it at Speedwellresearch.com. Members of Speedwell will get access not only to that research report, but about a dozen others as well. As a reminder, we spend several
hundred hours on every single one of our research reports, and one of the features of our research reports is a pretty extensive
history section. And what you will be listening to right now is an excerpt of that history section from our
coupon research report. If you prefer to read, though, instead of listen to this, you can find this at speedwell memos.com,
and if you want the full report, you can subscribe or buy a single report at speedwellresearch.com.
And without further ado, let us begin.
Founding History
In 1978, Bomb Kim was born in Seoul, South Korea.
His father worked for Hyundai construction and would commonly work outside of Korea to support Hyundai's
growing international business.
When Baumkim was seven, the family moved to America.
He would attend a boarding school in Massachusetts and later earn admission to Harvard
college, where his entrepreneurial impulse quickly became apparent. His first venture
was current magazine of four students, written by students, publication that he sold to Newsweek
in 2001. After graduating Harvard, in a short stint at the Boston Consulting Group, his entrepreneurial
drive drew him back into the media industry. Sticking with what worked the last time, he raised
4 million to create a Harvard alum magazine, dubbed 02138, after Cambridge's
zip code. It folded in the midst of the 2009 financial crisis, but not before Baumkim sold it,
protecting his investors from the worst of outcomes. He headed back to Harvard to attend their MBA program
to buy himself some time to come up with his next idea. Given his Korean roots, he wondered
whether there was a business in the U.S. that could do well in Korea.
Allowing him to marry his desire to create a business with his knowledge of the native culture,
it didn't take long for him to come up with something. Just six months after starting,
he dropped out of Harvard. At the time, Groupon, a popular startup focused on daily deals,
boomed with attention. The startup was so popular that it essentially marked the end of
post-financial crisis VC funding slump. VCs weren't just clamoring to
invest in Groupon. They were happy to throw money at any and all copycats. Part of Bomb Kim's impetus
to start a company in Korea was the idea that entrepreneurship was less prominent, at least compared to the
U.S., which also implied that there would be less competition. However, this couldn't have
been further from the truth. He would become the some 30th-odd entrepreneur.
to try to create a coupon clone in Korea. Nevertheless, the funding frenzy
meant getting started was easy. He raised an initial 2 million from investors, including Harvard
alum Bill Ackman, and moved back to Korea. He settled on coupon for the company's name, a play on
coupon, and the Korean Automanopoeia for fun, or surprise. Next section, business history.
In 2010, their first year of business, coupong generated 10 million in sales
with over 3 million customers. This incredible performance was in part due to the steep discounts users
could get on products and the fad-like novelty of the business model, but also because of Baum Kim's
ingenuity. He became one of the first Facebook advertisers in Korea and blanketed
the country with digital ads. Recognizing the power of Facebook early,
Didn't just mean a differentiated channel, but also incredibly cheap ads.
CPMs were so cheap that coupon was able to show every Korean 72 coupon ads a month.
With such visibility, they cinched a top spot amongst competitors such as Ticket Monster, We Make Price,
and Groupon Korea, despite launching several months after.
At the time, Baum Kim thought of the Daily Deal's platform as a demand-generating
generating platform, noting in the Korean Daily, in the traditional sense of commerce,
you needed something so you went shopping, but in social commerce, you see a good bargain and suddenly you need it,
and all the while you are socializing on the web. He would learn, like many entrepreneurs before him,
that getting a sale and giving consumers a great experience, can be worlds away.
This is particularly true when the business relies on discounting, which can spur and
purchases, usually at a cost of higher rates of consumer regret thereafter.
While coupon could easily acquire customers with very cheap customer acquisition cost, what they were offering
was unsustainable. Customers were largely interested in the steep discounts and merchants were only
happy to play along until they figured out that the immense traffic the Daily Deal brought
them seldom translated into positive economics.
coupon, like other daily deal-type businesses, was quite successful at getting
consumers onto their site. After all, who doesn't like 50% off? And similarly, most merchants were very receptive
to the potential boost in traffic. The way it worked was a merchant would offer a steeply discounted
deal contingent on a minimum number of customers participating. In the picture below, a merchant
is offering a 50% discount contingent on getting 100 people to participate
in the deal. As a consumer, you first sign up for the deal and put in your credit card info, but are only
charged for the deal once the minimum number of customers join it. Since you only get the deal if you
reach a critical point of participation, you are incentivized to share the deal with friends and on social
media. After the deal, quote, tips, tips, meaning the minimum number of customers are reached,
you are charged the discounted 50% off, or 24,700 won in this example, and receive a coupon
to redeem your deal in person. The proceeds received are then split between the merchant and coupon.
Prenticeses, the split varies, but on average, Groupon took 40%. Coupon was lower at 15%. Assuming
a 15% coupon take rate, the merchant in this case is effectively getting 42.5 cents
on the dollar of what they usually charge for this meal. Given the low gross margins of most restaurants,
this means that the merchant is likely losing money on the deal and hopes for two things that can
make this make sense. One, they can upsell the customer other items that they can make money on,
and two, the customer is going to come back even without a promotion. If it was
indeed a just one-time discount to get reoccurring business, then a local merchant
would run the deal and lose some money initially, but then have a larger regular customer base that
paid full price, giving them a sustainable business boost. The lifetime value of the customer
would be far more than its one-time customer acquisition cost. What actually happened
was the deal worked too well to attract customers, and all of the discounting-induced
traffic squeezed into such a short period of time usually meant an overwhelmed
restaurant. The influx of traffic would swamp the staff to the point that they couldn't offer proper customer
service. To get the customers fed quicker, the overworked staff would often yell,
Group on customer, when they entered to expedite the meal. However, that made the diners
feel like second-class customers. The large groups of people coming at one time also
meant longer wait times to get food, further aggravating customers. The customers
customers themselves were also usually price conscious and seldom added to their order beyond what was
included in the deal. And rather than becoming a new loyal customer, they moved on to participate
in the next deal. As merchants realized this was not going to bring back lasting business,
they either rolled back their discounts or stopped listing daily deals altogether. The smaller
deal selection, with lower discounts, would mean a worse daily deal offering
for consumers. If consumers' interests waned, then merchants would stop bothering listing on the platform
altogether. Compounding the issue is the fact that the daily deal business model relied on local
businesses, so there was a limited pool of merchants that they could churn through before they ran out.
This meant that no matter how quickly they could add businesses, as long as they
experienced tie churn, they would eventually be unable to replace the lost listings.
Furthermore, even if merchants stayed on the platform, they were limited by their small size and how much
they could offer in discounts. Nevertheless, despite the brewing issues with the business model,
they were thriving. Coupon was not only run-rating $300 million in annualized revenue
by the middle of 2011, but was also a high gross margin business with positive cash flow dynamics, as
customers paid in advance for each deal.
Baum Kim's initial solution to solve for the potential flaws in the daily deal model was modest.
He would start broadening their offerings to include product sales so merchants could sell
on their online website. They would offer discounted products for three to four days at a time,
which drove consumer impulsivity. And their large user base, which exceeded 5 million by
then, attracted a lot of merchants with clearance products. At the time, they
would describe the business as, quote, discovery shopping. To quote,
bomb came in 2011, people who come to coupon haven't decided what they want. They want to discover deals.
The idea of coupon as a demand generator that had a large audience that could sell whatever they
wanted, provided it was discounted, was thought of as a business virtue, since they
could sell things others couldn't. Despite stiff competition from Ticket Monster
and Groupon Korea, coupon became the number one player in the space.
Their relatively cheap customer acquisition cost and the fact that they received money for the daily deal up front
front helped them become cash flow positive early on. Just three years after founding, in 2013,
they set course for an IPO. But something was wrong. While the business was okay
financially, the business model had fundamental issues.
Selling products and services to highly price-sensitive customers in a gamified way, with pressure to close a sale,
hardly created lasting customer satisfaction. Additionally, alongside the idea of, quote, discovery
shopping came the fact that they often were selling things customers didn't really need.
Bomb Kim thought this would eventually catch up to them and decided he didn't want to
dedicate his life to building a company that served mediocrity.
Here's a quote from a 2018 Business Insider interview, recalling this period.
We don't believe that a company should exist or that a company should be created to strive for a
5 to 10% better customer experience. It's just a waste of our passion, our time, talents, our vision,
our goal. What we aspire to is to create a customer experience that is a
hundred times better. Six months into their IPO process, in just
mere weeks before the prospectus was supposed to be printed, Baum Kim had a moment of clarity and pivoted
the business. Bom Kim thought, if we really wanted to provide something that really mattered to customers,
a hundred times better, exponentially better, we had to go through an enormous amount of change.
They pulled the IPO, knowing they would have to remain private for the immense business shift
and heavy investment period they were about to undertake.
The third-party marketplace they operated offered an inconsistent experience, with a variety of different sellers
and limited logistics coverage nationally.
The mixed merchant experience, combined with unreliant shipping,
prentices, half of all complaints, were about shipping, helped clarify what coupon would need to build to build
in order to achieve 100x better experience.
Koupong would mimic Amazon by building out a large first-party offering and their own logistics network.
They went on to raise $100 million from Sequoia Capital in May 2014, and then another $300 million from BlackRock, a few months later,
to build out their logistics network and refine their mobile capabilities, which then was 80% of traffic.
They first focused on diapers and other categories for moms, with the logic, with the logic that
this new period of change usually creates a window for new habits to form.
In 2014, they launched Rocket Delivery, which was their company-owned delivery service that directly
employed drivers. The delivery force didn't just help them improve the shipping experience, it also gave
them an opportunity to interface with their customers. The quote, Rocket Men, as they were called,
became known for conscientious deliveries, knowing when to avoid ringing the doorbell,
so to not awaken a sleeping baby, and leaving hand-ridden notes for new mothers.
This did not come without a steep cost, though. They were rumored to have been burning hundreds of millions annually.
For someone familiar with the Amazon model, and comfortable with the losses,
that would prove to be no barrier to invest.
In 2015, SoftBank invested $1 billion in coupons.
which would allow them to continue to invest in their logistics network.
By 2016, they had over 3,600 rocket couriers, who boasted an incredibly high MPS score of 97.
Long gone were the days where shipping constituted the majority of complaints.
However, coupons still wanted to continue to improve delivery times to get them even faster.
In stark contrast to his earlier comments on how people who came to coupon
didn't know what they wanted, and it was coupon's role to effectively direct them
with deeply discounted deals, Baum Kim started saying, we can't bend the customers to what we want,
but we can bend ourselves to what the customer wants. The 1P model they adopted meant that all inventory
would be purchased directly by coupon, and steep deals and overstocks were no longer part of that
equation. What mattered was this concludes the free excerpt of a report.
